problems.title: Problem 1: Kinetic theory of real gases
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (75 points)

Kinetic theory of real gases

In the air at the Earth's surface, more than $10^{19}$ gas molecules per $1\,\mathrm{cm^3}$ fly around with speeds of several $100\,\mathrm{m/s}$. The pressure that a gas confined in a container exerts on the walls of the container is due to the forces exerted when such a large number of gas molecules collide with the walls of the container. If the motion of each individual gas molecule obeys classical mechanics, then by solving the equations of motion of the gas molecules one can obtain the trajectories of the individual gas molecules, and from them one can study macroscopic quantities such as pressure, and changes of state of the gas. Below, we examine how the mechanics of microscopic particles such as gas molecules gives rise to macroscopic physical quantities such as pressure.

[I] Kinetic theory of a gas of free particles

Consider a gas consisting of $N$ molecules confined in a spherical container of radius $R$. Below, the gas molecules can be regarded as point masses of mass $m$, and we call them particles. First, consider the case in which the particles exert no forces on each other and move freely. The particles are numbered by $i$, and particle $i$ moves with speed $v_i$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-1-fig1.png

Fig. 1.

Q1. When particle $i$ collides with the wall of the spherical container at angle of incidence $\theta_i$, find the magnitude of the change in the momentum of the particle in one collision. You may assume that the collisions between the particles and the wall of the container are elastic.

Q2. Find the number of times that particle $i$ of Q1 collides with the wall of the container during a time $\Delta t$. From this, find the force $F_i$, where $F_i\Delta t$ is the total magnitude of the impulse, in the direction perpendicular to the wall surface, that particle $i$ gives to the wall during the time $\Delta t$.

Q3. Show that the force per unit area (pressure) $P$ that the wall of the container receives from the collisions of the particles satisfies the relation

$$PV=\frac{2}{3}K \qquad (1)$$

where $V$ is the volume of the container and $K$ is the sum of the kinetic energies of the particles,

$$K=\sum_{i=1}^{N}\frac{1}{2}m{v_i}^2 .$$

The equation of state of an ideal gas is given, using the Boltzmann constant $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ and the absolute temperature $T$, by

$$PV=Nk_{\mathrm{B}}T .$$

From this and the result of Q3, the average kinetic energy per particle is given by

$$\frac{1}{2}m\overline{v^2}=\frac{3}{2}k_{\mathrm{B}}T \qquad (2)$$

and we see that it is related to the temperature, a macroscopic physical quantity. Here

$$\overline{v^2}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}{v_i}^2$$

is called the mean square of the particle velocities.

Q4. The atomic weight of the noble-gas element Ar (argon) is 39.9. From this, for Ar atoms in Ar gas at $T=300\ \mathrm{K}$, calculate the square root of the mean square velocity, $\sqrt{\overline{v^2}}$, as a measure of the particle speed. The Boltzmann constant $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ is $1.38\times10^{-23}\ \mathrm{J/K}$ and the Avogadro constant is $6.02\times10^{23}/\mathrm{mol}$.

[II] Motion of microscopic particles and long-time averages

Next, we consider the relation between the motion of microscopic particles and the observed quantities obtained as macroscopic physical quantities. Below, the position coordinate, velocity and acceleration of particle $i$ at time $t$ are denoted by $\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)$, $\overrightarrow{v_i}(t)$, $\overrightarrow{a_i}(t)$, respectively. By the equation of motion, the force acting on particle $i$ is $\overrightarrow{F_i}(t)=m\overrightarrow{a_i}(t)$.

When the behaviour of microscopic particles is observed, we consider that the observed macroscopic physical quantity corresponds to the long-time average of the corresponding physical quantity $Q(t)$ of the microscopic particles,

$$\lim_{T_{\mathrm{obs}}\to\infty}\frac{1}{T_{\mathrm{obs}}}\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{obs}}}Q(t)\,\mathrm{d}t=\langle Q\rangle .$$

We therefore consider integrating the physical quantity $Q(t)=\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)\cdot\overrightarrow{F_i}(t)$ from time $t=0$ to $t=T_{\mathrm{obs}}$. Here $\overrightarrow{A}\cdot\overrightarrow{B}$ denotes the inner product (scalar product) of the vectors $\overrightarrow{A}$ and $\overrightarrow{B}$.

Q5. Show, using the equation of motion, that the relation

$$\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{obs}}}\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)\cdot\overrightarrow{F_i}(t)\,\mathrm{d}t=m\Big[\overrightarrow{r_i}(T_{\mathrm{obs}})\cdot\overrightarrow{v_i}(T_{\mathrm{obs}})-\overrightarrow{r_i}(0)\cdot\overrightarrow{v_i}(0)\Big]-m\int_0^{T_{\mathrm{obs}}}|\overrightarrow{v_i}(t)|^2\,\mathrm{d}t$$

holds.

Q6. By dividing the result of Q5 by $T_{\mathrm{obs}}$ and then letting the observation time $T_{\mathrm{obs}}$ tend to infinity, we obtain the long-time average of the particle motion $\big\langle\overrightarrow{r_i}\cdot\overrightarrow{F_i}\big\rangle$. In this process the first term on the right-hand side of the equation of Q5, $m\Big[\overrightarrow{r_i}(T_{\mathrm{obs}})\cdot\overrightarrow{v_i}(T_{\mathrm{obs}})-\overrightarrow{r_i}(0)\cdot\overrightarrow{v_i}(0)\Big]$, does not contribute to the long-time average; explain the reason. By summing the quantity obtained in this way over all particles, with $K$ as the long-time average of the sum of the kinetic energies of the particles, the relation

$$\left\langle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overrightarrow{r_i}\cdot\overrightarrow{F_i}\right\rangle=\boxed{\mathtt{A}}\times K$$

is obtained. Give the number that goes into $\boxed{\mathtt{A}}$.

Q7. Let us apply this result to the case of free particles. The only forces acting on the particles are the forces that the particles receive from the wall at collisions. If the origin of the position vectors is taken at the centre of the spherical container, a particle receives a force directed towards the centre of the container (in the direction of $-\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)$) when $|\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)|=R$. From this, show that, using the pressure $P$ and the volume of the sphere $V=\dfrac{4\pi}{3}R^3$, one can write

$$\left\langle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overrightarrow{r_i}\cdot\overrightarrow{F_i}\right\rangle=\boxed{\mathtt{B}}\times PV$$

and give the number that goes into $\boxed{\mathtt{B}}$.

The quantity on the left-hand side of the equations of Q6 and Q7 is called the virial, and the equation of Q6, which shows the relation between the sum of the kinetic energies of the particles and the virial, is sometimes called the virial theorem. From the results of Q6 and Q7, the relation (1), which holds for the free particles obtained in [I], is obtained.

[III] Kinetic theory of a gas of interacting particles

Next, consider the case in which, in addition to the forces received from the wall, intermolecular forces (forces received from other molecules) act on the particles. That is, the force $\overrightarrow{F_i}$ acting on particle $i$ is written as

$$\overrightarrow{F_i}(t)=\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{wall}}(t)+\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{int}}(t)$$

where $\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{wall}}(t)$ and $\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{int}}(t)$ are, respectively, the force that particle $i$ receives from the wall and the force that particle $i$ receives from the particles other than $i$. As for the sum $K$ of the kinetic energies on the right-hand side of the equation of Q6, it is known that the relation (2) between the average kinetic energy and the absolute temperature $T$ holds even when intermolecular forces act. Also, since the contribution of the force $\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{wall}}(t)$ received from the wall to the virial is expressed in terms of the pressure by the result of Q7, we obtain

$$PV=Nk_{\mathrm{B}}T+\frac{1}{3}\left\langle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overrightarrow{r_i}\cdot\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{int}}\right\rangle \qquad (3)$$

Here the second term on the right-hand side represents the deviation from an ideal gas; below we estimate this term.

Q8. Considering that the intermolecular forces arise from forces acting between two particles, consider the case in which

$$\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{int}}(t)=\sum_{j=1}^{N}\overrightarrow{f_{ij}}(t)$$

Here $\overrightarrow{f_{ij}}(t)$ is the force that particle $j$ exerts on particle $i$, and $\overrightarrow{f_{ii}}(t)=0$. Show that in this case

$$\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)\cdot\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{int}}(t)=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\sum_{j=1}^{N}\Big[\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)-\overrightarrow{r_j}(t)\Big]\cdot\overrightarrow{f_{ij}}(t) .$$

Consider the case in which the intermolecular force $\overrightarrow{f_{ij}}(t)$ that particle $j$ exerts on particle $i$ is parallel to the vector $\overrightarrow{r_{ij}}=\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)-\overrightarrow{r_j}(t)$ directed from particle $j$ to particle $i$, and its magnitude depends only on the distance between the particles $r_{ij}=|\overrightarrow{r_{ij}}|$, that is,

$$\overrightarrow{f_{ij}}=\frac{\overrightarrow{r_{ij}}}{r_{ij}}\,f(r_{ij}) .$$

Further, suppose that the magnitude of the force $f(r_{ij})$ is expressed, using a certain function $U(r)$, as

$$f(r)=-\frac{\mathrm{d}U(r)}{\mathrm{d}r} .$$

This function $U(r)$ is called the potential energy of the intermolecular force, and can be interpreted as the potential energy of a particle at distance $r$ from the particle under consideration. Then, from Q8, the virial is expressed as

$$\left\langle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)\cdot\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{int}}(t)\right\rangle=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left\langle\sideset{}{'}\sum_{j=1}^{N}r_{ij}\frac{\mathrm{d}U(r_{ij})}{\mathrm{d}r_{ij}}\right\rangle .$$

Here the prime on the sum over $j$ on the right-hand side, $\displaystyle\sideset{}{'}\sum_{j=1}^{N}$, indicates that the sum does not include the term $j=i$.

To obtain the equation of state from equation (3) using this, one has to calculate the long-time average on the right-hand side, which is difficult in general. We therefore assume that, as seen from particle $i$, the other particles are distributed uniformly in the region where the potential energy $U(r)$ is at most of the order of the average kinetic energy of the particles, and we estimate the long-time average approximately by the average over a uniform spatial distribution in the region $U(r)<k_{\mathrm{B}}T$.

$U(r)$ usually has a shape like that in Fig. 2: at small $r$ a large repulsive force acts ($f=-\dfrac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}r}>0$), and outside that a weak attractive force ($f<0$) acts. Let $r_{\mathrm{c}}$ be the distance at which $U(r)=k_{\mathrm{B}}T$, and assume that particles $j$ are uniformly distributed in the region $r_{ij}>r_{\mathrm{c}}$. The average number of particles at distance $r$ from the particle $i$ under consideration is given by the product of the volume $4\pi r^2\mathrm{d}r$ of the region enclosed by the sphere of radius $r$ and the sphere of radius $r+\mathrm{d}r$ (with $\mathrm{d}r$ a small length, a spherical shell of radius $r$ and thickness $\mathrm{d}r$) and the average number density of particles $\rho=\dfrac{N}{V}$, i.e. by $4\pi r^2\rho\,\mathrm{d}r$. From this the virial is expressed as

$$\left\langle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overrightarrow{r_i}(t)\cdot\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{int}}(t)\right\rangle=-\frac{1}{2}N\int_{r_{\mathrm{c}}}^{\infty}r\frac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}r}4\pi r^2\rho\,\mathrm{d}r .$$

Here, since the spatial average does not depend on particle $i$, the sum over $i$ has been replaced by the number of particles $N$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-1-fig2.png

Fig. 2.

Q9. Show that from this expression the virial is given by

$$\left\langle\sum_{i=1}^{N}\overrightarrow{r_i}\cdot\overrightarrow{F_i}^{\mathrm{int}}\right\rangle=-\frac{3V}{2}\left(\frac{N}{V}\right)^2\left[-k_{\mathrm{B}}T\frac{4\pi}{3}r_c^3-4\pi\int_{r_c}^{\infty}r^2U(r)\,\mathrm{d}r\right]$$

where $r^3U(r)\to0$ as $r\to\infty$.

Q10. For systems with weak intermolecular forces, such as the noble-gas elements, the Lennard-Jones potential

$$U(r)=4\varepsilon\left[\left(\frac{d}{r}\right)^{12}-\left(\frac{d}{r}\right)^{6}\right]$$

is often adopted as the potential of the intermolecular force. Here $\varepsilon$ and $d$ are positive quantities, having the magnitudes of the binding energy of two particles and of the order of the particle diameter, respectively. Using this potential and approximating the lower limit $r_c$ of the integral in the expression obtained in Q9 by $d$, the equation of state obtained from equation (3) can be arranged in the form

$$PV=Nk_{\mathrm{B}}T-V\left(\frac{N}{V}\right)^2(a-bk_{\mathrm{B}}T) \qquad (4)$$

Find the mathematical expressions corresponding to $a$ and $b$.

Q11. For real gases, the equation of state

$$P+a\left(\frac{N}{V}\right)^2=\frac{Nk_{\mathrm{B}}T}{V-Nb} \qquad (5)$$

has been proposed and is called the van der Waals equation of state. Here $a$ and $b$ are constants; the second term on the left-hand side, containing $a$, represents the correction due to the intermolecular attraction, and the term $Nb$ in the denominator on the right-hand side represents the effect of the excluded volume, by which the space in which the gas molecules can move around becomes smaller because of the intermolecular repulsion. Show that when the excluded volume $Nb$ in the van der Waals equation of state is sufficiently small compared with the total volume $V$, that is, when $\dfrac{Nb}{V}\ll1$, the equation of state (5) can be expressed in the form of equation (4). You may use the approximation $(1+x)^{-1}\fallingdotseq1-x$ for $|x|\ll1$.

Q12. For argon atoms, the parameters $\varepsilon$, $d$ of the Lennard-Jones potential are given as

$$\varepsilon=1.725\times10^{-21}\ \mathrm{J},\qquad d=3.410\times10^{-10}\ \mathrm{m}$$

Using these, calculate the values of the van der Waals parameters $a$, $b$. Here you may approximate $r_c$ by $d$. Also, in this case, evaluate, at standard conditions ($1$ atm $=1013\ \mathrm{hPa}$, $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}=273\ \mathrm{K}$), the ratio $\dfrac{a}{P}\left(\dfrac{N}{V}\right)^2$ of the correction term due to the intermolecular attraction to the pressure in the van der Waals equation of state, and the ratio $\dfrac{Nb}{V}$ of the excluded volume to the volume of the gas. The volume of 1 mole of an ideal gas at standard conditions is $22.4\,\mathrm{L}$, and since argon gas is close to an ideal gas, you may use the volume of the ideal gas when calculating the ratios of the corrections.

problems.title: Problem 2: Electrostatic Carnot cycle
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (75 points)

Electrostatic Carnot cycle

A capacitor is a device that stores charge on its positive and negative plates. The stored charge $Q$ and the potential difference $V$ between the plates are related by $Q=CV$. The constant $C$ is determined by the shape of the capacitor plates, their separation, etc., and is called the capacitance. In this problem we investigate the properties of circuits using capacitors.

[I] Electrostatic energy of a capacitor

As in Fig. 1, a battery of emf $V$, a capacitor of capacitance $C$, a resistor of resistance $R$ and two switches SW1, SW2 are connected. Starting from the state in which the charge of the capacitor is 0, SW2 is opened and SW1 is closed to charge the capacitor. After the charging is complete, SW1 is opened, and then SW2 is closed to discharge the capacitor.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-2-fig2.png

Fig. 2.

Q1. Find the work done by the battery until the charging of the capacitor is complete.

Q2. Let $t=0$ be the time at which SW2 is closed, let $Q(t)$ be the charge of the capacitor at time $t\geqq0$ (the charge of the upper plate in Fig. 1), and let $I(t)$ be the current flowing in the circuit (the arrow in Fig. 1 is the positive direction).

(a) From the condition that the sum of the potential differences around the closed circuit is 0, find the relation satisfied by $Q(t)$ and $I(t)$.

(b) By differentiating the above relation with respect to $t$, derive the differential equation satisfied by $I(t)$, that is, the expression of $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I(t)}{\mathrm{d}t}$ in terms of $I(t)$.

(c) Find the current $I(0)$ immediately after SW2 is closed, and find the solution $I(t)$ of the above differential equation.

(d) In the discharging process, by integrating with respect to time the Joule heat generated in the resistor per unit time, $R\big(I(t)\big)^2$, find the Joule heat generated up to time $T(>0)$.

The total Joule heat due to the discharge, obtained by letting $T\to\infty$ in the above result, does not depend on the resistance $R$, and can be understood as the energy of the electric field (electrostatic energy) possessed by the charged capacitor. Then there is a difference between the work done by the battery and the energy possessed by the charged capacitor, and it appears that the law of conservation of energy is violated. This is because, in the process of charging the capacitor, we did not take into account the circuit resistance that is always present in a circuit and the Joule heat generated there.

Let us reconsider the process in which the battery charges the capacitor, using Fig. 2, to which the circuit resistance (resistance $r$) has been added.

Q3. Let $t=0$ be the time at which the switch SW is closed, let $Q(t)$ be the charge of the capacitor at time $t\geqq0$ (the charge of the upper plate in Fig. 2, $Q(0)=0$), and let $I(t)$ be the current flowing in the circuit (the arrow in Fig. 2 is the positive direction).

(a) From the condition that the sum of the potential differences around the closed circuit is 0, find the relation satisfied by $Q(t)$ and $I(t)$.

(b) By differentiating this relation with respect to $t$, derive the differential equation satisfied by $I(t)$.

(c) Find the value of the initial condition $I(0)$, and find the solution $I(t)$ of the above differential equation.

(d) How much Joule heat is generated in the circuit resistance during charging, up to time $T(>0)$?

If we let $T\to\infty$ in the above result, we see that the work done by the battery during charging becomes the Joule heat in the circuit resistance and the energy of the capacitor, and the law of conservation of energy is satisfied. Moreover, since this conclusion does not depend on the circuit resistance $r$, it does not depend on how fast the charging is.

[II] Charge transfer without energy loss

The Joule heat in the circuit resistance generated when a capacitor is charged is an energy loss accompanying the charging. Such losses occur not only in charging but whenever charge is transferred, so we consider a way to eliminate them. Below, the capacitor is a parallel-plate capacitor, and you may use the fact that the electrostatic energy $U$ of the capacitor is $U=\dfrac{Q^2}{2C}=\dfrac{1}{2}QV=\dfrac{1}{2}CV^2$, where $C$ is the capacitance, $Q$ the charge and $V$ the potential difference of the capacitor.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-2-fig3.png

Fig. 3.

The circuit of Fig. 3 (circuit resistance $r$) is prepared. The left plate of the capacitor is fixed to the apparatus, but the right plate can be moved left and right from outside, changing the plate separation. Let $C(x)$ be the capacitance when the position of the right plate is $x$. With the position of the right plate at $x$, the switch SW is closed, and after a sufficiently long time the charge $Q$ is stored on the right plate.

From this state, SW is opened and the position of the right plate is moved from $x$ by a small amount $\mathrm{d}x$; then the potential difference $V$ of the capacitor (the potential of the right plate relative to the left plate) changed by a small amount $\mathrm{d}V$. In this process the charge of the capacitor does not change, so it is called an isocharge process.

Q4. In this small isocharge process, we calculate the small mechanical work $\mathrm{d}W_Q$ that the capacitor does on the outside through the motion of the right plate.

(a) Express the force $F(x)$ due to the electric field acting on the right plate when the right plate is at position $x$ in a form proportional to $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}C}{\mathrm{d}x}$. The positive direction of the force $F$ is the direction of increasing $x$. (Hint: the force acting on the plate is the rate of change of the energy of the system when the plate is moved, with a minus sign.)

(b) Calculate the small work $\mathrm{d}W_Q$ from $\mathrm{d}W_Q=F(x)\mathrm{d}x$, write it in a form proportional to $\mathrm{d}V$, and express the proportionality coefficient using appropriate ones of $Q$, $V$.

In this isocharge process no current flows and no energy loss due to the circuit resistance $r$ occurs, so the work that the capacitor did on the outside is equal to the decrease of the electrostatic energy of the capacitor.

Next, after returning the plate to position $x$, SW is closed. Closing SW causes no transfer of charge, and the force acting on the plate does not change either. After that, when the plate is moved from position $x$ to $x+\mathrm{d}x$, a small charge $\mathrm{d}Q$ is added to the capacitor, and the charge of the right plate becomes $Q+\mathrm{d}Q$. In this process the potential difference $V$ of the capacitor is fixed, so it is called an isopotential process.

Q5. In this small isopotential process, we calculate the small mechanical work $\mathrm{d}W_V$ that the capacitor does on the outside through the motion of the right plate.

(a) The work $\mathrm{d}W_V=F(x)\mathrm{d}x$ is the same amount as the work $\mathrm{d}W_Q$ found in the previous question. Write the work $\mathrm{d}W_V$ in a form proportional to $\mathrm{d}Q$, and express the proportionality coefficient using appropriate ones of $Q$, $V$.

(b) In this isopotential process, write the work $\mathrm{d}P$ done by the battery and the change $\mathrm{d}U$ of the electrostatic energy of the capacitor in forms proportional to $\mathrm{d}Q$, and express each proportionality coefficient using appropriate ones of $Q$, $V$.

As can be seen from the above results, when the charge is increased or decreased in this isopotential process, there is no Joule heat loss due to the circuit resistance. Since this conclusion is derived from relations between small quantities, the operation of changing the position of the plate (increasing or decreasing the capacitance) must be performed sufficiently slowly. This fact corresponds to the general property that a quasi-static process (a process in which the change of state is performed sufficiently slowly while maintaining equilibrium) is a reversible process (not accompanied by the generation of Joule heat).

[III] Electrostatic Carnot cycle

As in Fig. 4, a capacitor whose capacitance can be changed by moving its right plate and two batteries of emf $V_1$ and $V_2$ ($V_1<V_2$) are connected with two switches SW1, SW2. By repeating isopotential processes and isocharge processes, mechanical and electrical work can be exchanged between the capacitor and the outside. Because of the analogy with a heat engine, in this problem this system is called the electrostatic Carnot cycle.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-2-fig4.png

Fig. 4.

The state of the capacitor is specified by the two variables: its charge $Q$ (the charge of the right plate) and the potential difference $V$ (the potential of the right plate relative to the left plate). One cycle is performed by carrying out the following four processes in succession. In all the processes, the operation of changing the position of the plate is performed sufficiently slowly.

1) A$\to$B: In state A, SW1 is closed and SW2 is open. The charge of the capacitor is $Q_1$ and the potential difference is $V_1$. SW1 is opened and the plate position is moved so that the potential difference increases to $V_2$.

2) B$\to$C: SW2 is closed and the plate position is moved so that the charge increases to $Q_2$.

3) C$\to$D: SW2 is opened and the plate position is moved so that the potential difference decreases to $V_1$.

4) D$\to$A: SW1 is closed and the plate position is moved so that the charge decreases to $Q_1$, returning to state A.

Q6. On the $Q$-$V$ diagram of the answer sheet, draw the above cycle with a solid line, clearly marking the positions of the states A, B, C, D.

Q7. In a certain change of state, let $\varDelta U$ be the increase of the electrostatic energy of the capacitor, $\varDelta P$ the energy supply (electrical work) from the external system to the capacitor through the circuit, and $\varDelta W$ the mechanical work that the capacitor does on the outside through the right plate. These physical quantities are not small quantities.

(a) Write the relation that holds among the three quantities $\varDelta U$, $\varDelta P$, $\varDelta W$.

(b) For each of the four processes of the cycle, express $\varDelta U$, $\varDelta P$, $\varDelta W$ using appropriate ones of $Q_1$, $Q_2$, $V_1$, $V_2$.

Q8. We examine the transfer of energy in this cycle [A$\to$B$\to$C$\to$D$\to$A].

(a) How much work does the capacitor do on the outside through the right plate in one cycle?

(b) Express in terms of $V_1$, $V_2$ the efficiency of this cycle, that is, the ratio of the work that the capacitor does on the outside to the energy (electrical work) supplied to the capacitor from the high-emf side.

Q9. When the reverse cycle [A$\to$D$\to$C$\to$B$\to$A], in which all the processes are reversed, is run, it operates as a pump carrying charge to the side of higher potential, and works as a device that charges the battery on the high-emf side. In this reverse cycle, let $C_{\min}$ be the minimum value and $C_{\max}$ the maximum value of the capacitance of the capacitor.

(a) In which of the states A, B, C, D is the capacitance minimum, and in which is it maximum? Express the charge transferred to the battery on the high-emf side in one reverse cycle using $V_1$, $V_2$, $C_{\max}$, $C_{\min}$.

(b) This reverse cycle is run at $3.0\times10^2$ Hz while the capacitance of the capacitor is changed by a factor of $5.0\times10^2$. With $V_1=0.60\mathrm{V}$, $V_2=5.0\mathrm{V}$, what is the maximum capacitance $C_{\max}$ of the capacitor needed to fully charge, in 24 hours, a mobile battery ($5.0\mathrm{V}$, $2.0\mathrm{Ah}$) connected on the $V_2$ side with this device, starting from the empty state? Give it to 2 significant figures, and state the unit. Assume that the emf of the mobile battery is constant regardless of the remaining charge. Ah (ampere-hour) is a unit of charge, used to express the capacity of a battery; 1 Ah denotes the capacity to draw a current of 1 A continuously for 1 hour.

[IV] Magnetic energy of a coil

Besides the method using the isopotential process of [II], another way to transfer charge without Joule heat loss is to use the magnetic energy stored in a coil. A coil is a device consisting of a conducting wire wound many times, which produces a magnetic field when a current $I$ flows. By the law of electromagnetic induction, when the current $I$ is changing, an emf $-L\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I}{\mathrm{d}t}$ is produced in the direction that opposes the change. The constant $L$ is called the self-inductance and is determined by the shape and the number of turns of the coil.

As in Fig. 5, a battery, a coil of self-inductance $L$, and resistors of resistance $R$ and $r$ are connected. After the switch SW is closed and a sufficiently long time has passed, the current flowing in the coil becomes a constant value $I_0$. After that, SW is opened at time $t=0$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-2-fig5.png

Fig. 5.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-2-fig6.png

Fig. 6.

Q10. We find the Joule heat generated in the resistor after SW is opened.

(a) Let $I(t)$ be the current flowing in the coil at time $t\geqq0$ (the direction of the arrow in Fig. 5 is positive). Derive the differential equation satisfied by $I(t)$, and find the solution satisfying the initial condition $I(0)=I_0$.

(b) By integrating with respect to time the Joule heat generated per unit time in the resistor of resistance $R$, $R\big(I(t)\big)^2$, find the Joule heat generated from time 0 to $T(>0)$.

The total Joule heat obtained by letting $T\to\infty$ in the above result does not depend on $R$, and can be regarded as the energy when the current $I_0$ flows in a coil of self-inductance $L$. This energy can be understood as the energy of the magnetic field produced by the current flowing in the coil.

As in Fig. 6, a circuit connecting two capacitors of capacitance $C_1$, $C_2$ is made. Initially, the charge of the left capacitor was $Q_1$ (on the upper plate), and the charge of the right capacitor was 0. When the switch SW is closed, the charges move and are redistributed so that the sum of the electrostatic energies of the two capacitors becomes minimum.

Q11. Let $U(Q)$ be the sum of the electrostatic energies of the two capacitors when a charge $Q$ has moved in the direction of the arrow in the figure. What is the $Q$ that minimizes $U(Q)$?

As the charge moves, the electrostatic energy decreases and reaches its minimum value. The decrease of the electrostatic energy must have become Joule heat generated by the circuit resistance present in the circuit.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-2-fig7.png

Fig. 7.

As in Fig. 7, a coil of self-inductance $L$ and a resistor representing the circuit resistance $r$ are added to the circuit of Fig. 6. Initially the charge of the left capacitor is $Q_1$ (on the upper plate) and the charge of the right capacitor is 0, and the switch SW is closed at time $t=0$. We examine what happens to the electrostatic energy in this circuit.

Let $I(t)$ be the current at time $t$ (the arrow in Fig. 7 is the positive direction), $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I(t)}{\mathrm{d}t}$ the rate of change of the current, $Q(t)$ the charge on the upper plate of the right capacitor, and $K(t)$ the magnetic energy of the coil. Also let $J(t)$ be the amount of Joule heat generated in the circuit resistance $r$ from time 0 to $t$.

Q12. Taking point A of the circuit as the reference point of potential (zero potential), let $V(t)$ be the potential of point B.

(a) Express $V(t)$ using $C_1$, $C_2$, $Q_1$, $Q(t)$.

(b) Express $V(t)$ using $L$, $r$, $I(t)$, $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}I(t)}{\mathrm{d}t}$.

Q13. Suppose that at time $t$, during a small time $\mathrm{d}t$, a small charge $\mathrm{d}Q$ flows in the circuit, and the charge of the right capacitor becomes $Q(t)+\mathrm{d}Q$.

(a) Find the rates of change of each of the following three physical quantities accompanying this transfer of charge $\mathrm{d}Q$.

• The rate of change $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}Q}$ of the sum $U$ of the electrostatic energies of the two capacitors

• The rate of change $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}K}{\mathrm{d}Q}$ of the energy $K$ of the magnetic field produced by the current flowing in the coil

• The rate of change $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}J}{\mathrm{d}Q}$ of the amount $J$ of Joule heat generated in the circuit resistance

(b) Using the expressions for the potential $V(t)$ found in the previous question, find the relation satisfied by $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}U}{\mathrm{d}Q}$, $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}K}{\mathrm{d}Q}$, $\dfrac{\mathrm{d}J}{\mathrm{d}Q}$, and state its physical meaning.

(c) When the circuit resistance is $r=0$, what is the maximum value $I_{\max}$ of the current flowing in the circuit?

Even if the circuit resistance $r$ is made to approach 0, the current flowing in the circuit remains finite, so Joule heat generation disappears. This is completely different from the situation calculated in Q3. In the circuit of Fig. 7, the charge at potential $V$ released from the lower plate of the right capacitor has its electrostatic energy converted into magnetic energy by the back emf of the coil, and reaches the lower plate of the left capacitor at potential 0. In this sense, the coil takes on the characteristic of the isopotential process of the previous section, realizing a transfer of charge without Joule heat loss.

problems.title: Problem 3: Optics related to lenses
problems.problem:
Problem 3 (75 points)

Optics related to lenses

[I] Measurement of the refractive index

When designing optical instruments made of glass or resin, the value of the refractive index of the material is needed. For a prism whose two faces have been precisely polished to an apex angle $\alpha$ ($<90^{\circ}$), we want to find the refractive index of the material by measuring the angle $\delta$ (the deviation angle) between the incident ray and the emerging ray.

Q1. Let $\theta_1$ be the angle of incidence on the prism and $\theta_2$ the exit angle from the prism (the angle of refraction of the light going out from the prism side). Express the deviation angle $\delta$ using $\theta_1$, $\theta_2$ and the apex angle $\alpha$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-3-fig1.png

Fig. 1. A prism with apex angle $\alpha$, the angle of incidence $\theta_1$, the exit angle $\theta_2$, and the deviation angle $\delta$, the angle between the incident ray and the emerging ray

Fig. 2 shows the relation between the angle of incidence $\theta_1$ and the deviation angle $\delta$ for $\alpha=60^{\circ}$, $n=1.50$. As can be seen from this figure, for a given apex angle and refractive index the deviation angle has a minimum value. Considering that the deviation angle does not change when the directions of incidence and emergence are interchanged, the deviation angle is minimum when the angle of incidence and the exit angle are equal. Making use of this, the refractive index $n$ of the material of the prism can be found by measuring the minimum deviation angle ($\delta_0$).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-3-fig2.png

Fig. 2. The relation between the angle of incidence $\theta_1$ and the deviation angle $\delta$ for $\alpha=60^{\circ}$, $n=1.50$

Q2. Express the refractive index $n$ of the prism in terms of the apex angle $\alpha$ of the prism and the minimum deviation angle $\delta_0$. The refractive index of air is 1.0.

[II] Thick lens

Consider a spherical biconvex lens made of a glass material of refractive index $n$, the radius of one face of which is $R_1\,(>0)$ and the radius of the other face is $R_2\,(>0)$. The straight line joining the centres of the two spherical surfaces is the optical axis, and the distance $d$ between the points of intersection of the optical axis with the respective spherical surfaces (the surface vertices) is defined as the thickness of the lens.

To consider the effect of the lens radius $R_1$ on the incident side for a ray entering the lens, consider the case $d\gg R_2$. Consider a ray that leaves a point on the optical axis at distance $a_1$ from the surface vertex and enters the lens surface at angle of incidence $\theta_1$. Let $b_1$ be the distance between the surface vertex and the point of intersection of the refracted ray with the optical axis. Assume that the angle $\alpha_1$ between the incident ray and the optical axis, the angle $\beta_1$ between the refracted ray and the optical axis, and the angle $\gamma_1$ between the optical axis and the straight line joining the point of incidence on the lens and the centre of curvature of the lens surface are all small, so that they can be approximated as

$$\begin{cases}\sin\alpha_1\fallingdotseq\alpha_1,\ \cos\alpha_1\fallingdotseq1\\ \sin\beta_1\fallingdotseq\beta_1,\ \cos\beta_1\fallingdotseq1\\ \sin\gamma_1\fallingdotseq\gamma_1,\ \cos\gamma_1\fallingdotseq1\end{cases}$$

(see Fig. 3). Then, from geometrical relations,

$$\begin{cases}\alpha_1\fallingdotseq\dfrac{R_1}{a_1}\gamma_1\\[2mm] \beta_1\fallingdotseq\dfrac{R_1}{b_1}\gamma_1\end{cases}$$

and likewise, from geometrical relations, the angle of incidence $\theta_1$ and the angle of refraction $\theta_1{}'$ are

$$\begin{cases}\theta_1=\alpha_1+\gamma_1\\ \theta_1{}'=\gamma_1-\beta_1\end{cases}$$

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-3-fig3.png

Fig. 3. Schematic diagram of the geometry of a ray entering the lens

By Snell's law, for small angles

$$\alpha_1+\gamma_1\fallingdotseq n\,(\gamma_1-\beta_1)$$

and therefore

$$\frac{R_1}{a_1}+1\fallingdotseq n\left(1-\frac{R_1}{b_1}\right)$$

That is, we find that the reciprocal $\dfrac{1}{b_1}$ of the distance $b_1$ can be expressed using the reciprocal $\dfrac{1}{a_1}$ of the distance $a_1$, the reciprocal $\dfrac{1}{R_1}$ of the radius $R_1$, and the refractive index $n$ as

$$\frac{1}{b_1}=\frac{1}{n}\left(\frac{n-1}{R_1}-\frac{1}{a_1}\right)$$

(where $a_1>\dfrac{R_1}{n-1}$).

Q3. To consider the effect of the lens radius $R_2$ on the exit side for a ray leaving the lens, consider the case $d\gg R_1$. Consider a ray that, from inside the lens, strikes the inner surface of the lens at angle of incidence $\theta_2'$. Let $b_2$ be the distance between the surface vertex and the point of intersection of the ray refracted by the lens with the optical axis. Also, let $a_2$ be the distance between the surface vertex and the point of intersection of the ray with the optical axis in the case where it is not refracted by the lens and goes straight on. Assume that the angle $\alpha_2$ between the optical axis and the ray in the hypothetical case where it goes straight on, the angle $\beta_2$ between the refracted ray and the optical axis, and the angle $\gamma_2$ between the optical axis and the straight line joining the exit point from the lens and the centre of curvature of the lens surface are all small, so that they can be approximated as

$$\begin{cases}\sin\alpha_2\fallingdotseq\alpha_2,\ \cos\alpha_2\fallingdotseq1\\ \sin\beta_2\fallingdotseq\beta_2,\ \cos\beta_2\fallingdotseq1\\ \sin\gamma_2\fallingdotseq\gamma_2,\ \cos\gamma_2\fallingdotseq1\end{cases}$$

(see Fig. 4). Express the reciprocal $\dfrac{1}{b_2}$ of the distance $b_2$ using the reciprocal $\dfrac{1}{a_2}$ of the distance $a_2$, the reciprocal $\dfrac{1}{R_2}$ of the radius $R_2$, and the refractive index $n$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-3-fig4.png

Fig. 4. Schematic diagram of the geometry of a ray leaving the lens

Q4. Noting that the thickness of the lens is $d=b_1-a_2$, express $d$ in terms of $R_1$, $R_2$, $a_1$, $b_2$ and the refractive index $n$.

Q5. Using that result, express the distance $b_2$ in the case $a_1\to\infty$ in terms of the refractive index $n$, $R_1$, $R_2$ and the thickness $d$ of the lens.

From here on, we want to consider how the thickness $d$ of the lens affects the focal length.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-3-fig5.png

Fig. 5. Schematic diagram of a ray incident on a thick lens parallel to the optical axis

Consider a ray incident parallel to the optical axis from infinity (corresponding to $a_1\to\infty$). The point of intersection of the ray after passing through the lens with the optical axis is the focal point (point F in Fig. 5). Consider a hypothetical lens of extremely small thickness that has the same trajectory as both the ray incident on the lens and the ray after passing through the lens, and define the distance from the position of that hypothetical lens to the focal point as the focal length of the thick lens. That is, consider the point of intersection (point G in Fig. 5) of the lines obtained by extending both the incident ray and the ray after passing through the lens towards the lens, and the point of intersection (point H in Fig. 5) of the optical axis with the perpendicular dropped from G to the optical axis; the distance from this point H to the focal point F is defined as the focal length $f$.

Q6. Express the angle $\alpha_2$ between the ray and the optical axis, in the case where the ray, on leaving the lens, is not refracted by the lens and hypothetically goes straight on, in terms of the refractive index $n$ of the lens material and the angle $\gamma_1$ between the optical axis and the normal to the lens surface at the point of incidence P on the lens.

Q7. Express the angle $\beta_2$ between the ray leaving the lens and the optical axis in terms of the refractive index $n$ of the lens material, the lens radius $R_1$ on the incident side, the distance $b_2$, the thickness $d$ of the lens, and the angle $\gamma_1$ between the optical axis and the normal to the lens surface at the point of incidence P on the lens.

Q8. Express the focal length $f$ in terms of the refractive index $n$ of the lens material, the lens radius $R_1$ on the incident side, the lens radius $R_2$ on the exit side, and the thickness $d$ of the lens.

[III] Depth of focus and depth of field

When taking a photograph with a camera, because the image sensor has a finite size, for a given distance $a$ from the lens to the object there is a certain range of distances $b$ from the lens of the image that can be accepted as an in-focus photograph. This range in which the image is in focus is called the "depth of focus". Conversely, on the object side as well, there is a certain range of distances that are in focus, and this range is called the "depth of field".

The human eye has an iris to adjust the amount of light received by the retina. Similarly, a camera is equipped with an "aperture stop", which adjusts the aperture diameter of the lens in order to adjust the amount of light received by the image sensor. Consider the case of a lens of focal length $f$. By changing the aperture diameter $D$, one can adjust the amount of light and at the same time change the depth of field and the spatial resolving power of the lens. We want to consider how the depth of field depends on the focal length $f$ of the lens and on the "f-number" $F=\dfrac{f}{D}$.

Let the distance from the lens to the object along the optical axis be $a_0$ ($<\infty$), and let the distances from the lens corresponding to the depth-of-field range be $a_0+\delta a_+$ on the far side and $a_0-\delta a_-$ on the near side ($\delta a_+,\ \delta a_-\ll a_0$). Let the distances from the lens to the corresponding image positions be $b_0$, $b_0-\delta b_+$, $b_0+\delta b_-$, respectively ($\delta b_+,\ \delta b_-\ll b_0$). Also, let $\varepsilon$ denote the "permissible circle of confusion", the size that can be accepted as in focus on the image plane at distance $b_0$ from the lens. That is, the size of the slight blur, at distance $b_0$ from the lens on the image-sensor side, of the light from distance $a_0+\delta a_+$ or $a_0-\delta a_-$ from the lens on the object side corresponds to $\varepsilon$ (see Fig. 6).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-3-fig6.png

Fig. 6. Schematic diagram of the geometry of the image positions $b_0$, $b_0-\delta b_+$, $b_0+\delta b_-$ of a lens of aperture diameter $D$ and the permissible circle of confusion $\varepsilon$ ($\ll D$)

Q9. Express the depth of focus $\varDelta b=\delta b_++\delta b_-$ using $b_0$, $\varepsilon$, the focal length $f$ of the lens, and the f-number $F$ of the lens.

Q10. For $a_0>f$, express the depth of field $\varDelta a=\delta a_++\delta a_-$ using $a_0$, $\varepsilon$, the focal length $f$ of the lens, and the f-number $F$ of the lens.

[IV] Diffraction limit

So far, the points through which light passes have been treated literally as points of infinitesimal area, and light has been treated as rays. In reality, the devices through which light passes, such as lenses and slits, have non-negligible sizes, and light also has the properties of a wave. Let us examine these effects.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-3-fig7.png

[円孔 = circular aperture; スクリーン = screen]

Fig. 7. Conceptual diagram of the arrangement of the circular aperture and the screen

Consider the case in which monochromatic light of wavelength $\lambda$ is incident perpendicularly on a circular aperture of diameter $D$, and consider the diffraction pattern on a screen placed parallel to the aperture at distance $L$ from it (see Fig. 7). The light reaching a point P on the screen at distance $q$ from the centre point O of the screen (the intersection of the perpendicular from the centre of the aperture with the screen) is the collection of the light that has passed through the various points of the aperture. Let us specify a point of the aperture by polar coordinates $(r,\phi)$ with the centre of the aperture as the origin. $r$ is the distance from the origin and $\phi$ is the polar angle, and the direction $\phi=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$ is taken parallel to $\overrightarrow{\mathrm{OP}}$. The path length $\ell(r,\phi)$ of the light that passes through the point with coordinates $(r,\phi)$ on the aperture and reaches the point P on the screen is approximated, using the distance between the centre of the aperture and the point P,

$$\ell_0=\left(L^2+q^2\right)^{1/2}$$

and further assuming $\ell_0\gg r$, as

$$\begin{aligned}\ell(r,\phi)&=\left\{L^2+(r\sin\phi-q)^2+r^2\cos^2\phi\right\}^{1/2}\\ &=\ell_0\left(1+\frac{-2qr\sin\phi+r^2}{{\ell_0}^2}\right)^{1/2}\\ &\fallingdotseq\ell_0\left(1-\frac{q}{{\ell_0}^2}\,r\sin\phi\right)\end{aligned}$$

Q11. The light at each point of the aperture has the same amplitude and the same phase; with the phase at time $t$ equal to $\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}ct$ ($c$ denotes the speed of light) and the amplitude $A$, the light wave there is written as

$$A\sin\left(\frac{2\pi}{\lambda}ct\right)$$

Then express the sum $\varPhi(r,t)$ of all the light that passes through the points of the ring of radius $r$ from the centre of the aperture in the aperture plane and reaches the point P, using $q$, $\ell_0$, $k=\dfrac{2\pi}{\lambda}$, $A$, $c$, $t$ and the radius $r$ of the ring. If necessary, you may use the formulas

$$\begin{cases}\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\cos(u\sin\phi)\,\mathrm{d}\phi=2\pi J_0(u)\\[3mm] \displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\sin(u\sin\phi)\,\mathrm{d}\phi=0\end{cases}$$

Here $J_0(u)$ is the function defined by

$$J_0(u)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(-1)^n\left(\dfrac{u}{2}\right)^{2n}}{(n!)^2}$$

(see Fig. 8).

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-3-fig8.png

Fig. 8. Left: the functions $J_0(u)$ and $J_1(u)$. Right: the functions $J_1(u)$ and $\dfrac{J_1(u)}{u}$

Q12. If the light $\varPhi(r,t)$ that passes through the ring of radius $r$ from the centre of the aperture and reaches the point P is integrated over $r$ from the centre up to the radius $\dfrac{D}{2}$ of the aperture, we obtain the total light that passes through the aperture and reaches the point P. Express the intensity of the light on the screen (proportional to the square of the amplitude), as a function of the visual angle $\theta=\dfrac{q}{\ell_0}$ from the centre of the aperture, using $k$, the diameter $D$ of the aperture, and $\theta$. Also, draw a rough sketch of the light intensity on the screen obtained in this way, taking $\dfrac{kD}{2}\theta$ as the variable of the horizontal axis. On the vertical axis, set the light intensity at the centre point O of the screen equal to 1. In doing so, you may use the formula

$$\int_0^{u}xJ_0(x)\,\mathrm{d}x=uJ_1(u)$$

and base your sketch on the form of the function $\dfrac{J_1(u)}{u}$ shown in the right-hand panel of Fig. 8.

An important thing learned from the above consideration is that, when the wave nature of light (diffraction of light) is taken into account, even when light is focused by a lens it does not converge to a single point but has a spread. Its degree depends only on the wavelength of the light and the aperture of the lens, and does not depend on the focal length, the magnification, the refractive index of the material, etc. Because of this spreading of light by diffraction, the images of two points closer together than a certain limiting value overlap, and the two can no longer be distinguished. This means that a lens has a limit to its resolving power. The minimum angle at which two neighbouring points can be distinguished as two independent points is called the "spatial resolving power of the lens".

Q13. Among the values of $u$ satisfying $J_1(u)=0$, the smallest one with $u\neq0$ is

$$u_1=3.832$$

(see Fig. 8). Considering the spread of light by the lens as the quantity corresponding to this $u_1$, express the spatial resolving power of the lens using the wavelength $\lambda$ of the light and the aperture $D$ of the lens.

Q14. What lens aperture is needed to distinguish an object of $1\,\mathrm{m}$ on the lunar surface from a lunar orbiting satellite at an altitude of $100\,\mathrm{km}$ above the lunar surface, using visible light of wavelength $500\,\mathrm{nm}$? Round up the digits after the decimal point and give the answer in units of cm.

problems.title: Problem 4: Dark energy
problems.problem:
Problem 4 (75 points)

Dark energy

[I] The law of conservation of mechanical energy and the Friedmann equation

Triggered by the discovery, in the first half of the 20th century, of the "Hubble–Lemaître (Hubble-Lemaitre) law" based on observations of distant galaxies, the fact that our universe is expanding became clear. Our universe, when averaged over very large scales, is homogeneous and isotropic (the "cosmological principle"), and, thinking naively, the expansion of the universe can be regarded as a phenomenon in which matter with a uniform mass distribution (celestial bodies, interstellar matter, etc.) spreads out uniformly with time. Let us therefore consider, as a simple mechanical model that can describe the expansion of the universe, a sphere that expands (or contracts) together with the universe.

For convenience, take the centre of this sphere as the origin O, and let $R(t)$ be the radius of the sphere at time $t$. $R(t)$ is a function of the time $t$ only, and the sphere expands or contracts uniformly while keeping its shape. The total mass inside the sphere is constant, and the (mass) density $\rho(t)$ inside the sphere changes with time as $R(t)$ increases or decreases, but is always uniform. To describe the expansion of the universe concisely, with $R_0\,(>0)$ the radius of the sphere at a certain time (the "present") $t=t_0$, the "scale factor" is defined as $a(t)=\dfrac{R(t)}{R_0}$. That is, the expansion of the universe can be regarded as a phenomenon in which the scale factor $a(t)$ increases monotonically.

In all the questions below, for a function $X(t)$ of time $t$, we use the abbreviations $\dot{X}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}X}{\mathrm{d}t}$, $\ddot{X}=\dfrac{\mathrm{d}^2X}{\mathrm{d}t^2}$.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2025-4-fig1.png

[質点 = point mass; 密度 = density]

Fig. 1. 'Sphere'

Q1. A point P located at time $t$ at distance $r(t)\,(\le R(t))$ from the centre O moves, as the sphere expands or contracts, keeping the ratio of $r(t)$ to $R(t)$ fixed. Defining $H(t)=\dfrac{\dot{a}(t)}{a(t)}$, express the velocity $v(t)=\dot{r}(t)$ of the point P at time $t$ using $H(t)$ and $r(t)$.

This expresses the "Hubble–Lemaître law" mentioned at the beginning.

Q2. Based on Newton's law of universal gravitation, find the equation of motion and the law of conservation of mechanical energy for a point mass placed on the surface of the sphere, and, writing them as

$$\ddot{a}=F(a), \qquad (\mathrm{I.1})$$

$$\frac{1}{2}\dot{a}^2+U(a)=E \qquad (\mathrm{I.2})$$

express the functions $F(a)$, $U(a)$ of $a$ using $\rho_0=\rho(t_0)$, the gravitational constant $G$, etc. ($E$ is a constant. Here the origin of $U(a)$ is fixed by $\displaystyle\lim_{a\to\infty}U(a)=0$.) You may find the gravitational force acting on the point mass on the surface of the sphere by regarding the total mass of the sphere as concentrated at the centre O. Also, by differentiating both sides of equation (I.2) with respect to $t$ and comparing with equation (I.1), find the relation between $F(a)$ and $U(a)$.

In this model we see that the expansion of the universe is always a decelerating expansion ($\ddot{a}<0$).

In more rigorous cosmology, the expansion of the universe is investigated using the "Friedmann equation" derived from general relativity. The Friedmann equation is an equation that relates $H(t)=\dfrac{\dot{a}(t)}{a(t)}$ to the "energy density" of the universe (energy per unit volume) and describes the time variation of the scale factor $a(t)$; in the naive model of cosmic expansion considered here it is written as follows:

$$\frac{H^2}{H_0^2}=\frac{\varOmega_{\mathrm{m}}}{a^3}+\frac{1-\varOmega_{\mathrm{m}}}{a^2} \qquad (\mathrm{I.3})$$

Here we have put $H_0=H(t_0)$ (the "Hubble constant"). Also, $\varOmega_{\mathrm{m}}\,(\ge0)$ is a dimensionless constant representing the relative energy density at $t=t_0$, and is called the "density parameter". The first term on the right-hand side is proportional to the energy density $\varepsilon(t)$, and the second term represents the effect of the curvature ('degree of bending') of the universe. (Since the left-hand side of equation (I.3) equals 1 at $t=t_0$, the coefficient of the second term on the right-hand side has been chosen so as not to contradict this fact.)

In modern "observational cosmology", determining constants such as $H_0$ and $\varOmega_{\mathrm{m}}$ by observation is an important theme. Here, for $H_0$ we use the measured value determined from measurements of the distances to distant galaxies and their recession velocities (the speeds at which they move away from our galaxy), while $\varOmega_{\mathrm{m}}$ is treated as a parameter.

Q3. The Friedmann equation (I.3) can be reproduced from the law of conservation of mechanical energy (I.2) considered in Q2. By comparing equation (I.3) with the result of Q2, express the proportionality constant $A$ in $\rho_0=A\varOmega_{\mathrm{m}}$ in terms of $H_0$, and further find it to 2 significant figures using the necessary ones of the following numerical values. Take the unit of $A$ to be $\mathrm{kg/m^3}$.

$H_0=70\,\mathrm{km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}=2.27\times10^{-18}\,\mathrm{s^{-1}}$, $\quad 1\,\mathrm{Mpc}=10^{6}\,\mathrm{pc}=3.09\times10^{22}\,\mathrm{m}$, $G=6.67\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{m^3\,kg^{-1}\,s^{-2}}$

(The pc (parsec) is a unit of distance used as standard in astrophysics. 1 pc is equal to about 3.26 light years, and the average distance between stars in the Milky Way Galaxy is of this order.)

Q4. Let $t=0$ be the instant at which the universe began (the "Big Bang"), and let $a(t)>0$, $\displaystyle\lim_{t\to+0}a(t)=0$. Assuming that the universe continues to expand forever, find the maximum value $\varOmega_{\mathrm{m,\,max}}$ that the density parameter $\varOmega_{\mathrm{m}}$ can take, by interpreting the Friedmann equation (I.3) as the law of conservation of mechanical energy (I.2). Also, when $\varOmega_{\mathrm{m}}>\varOmega_{\mathrm{m,\,max}}$, the universe turns from expansion to contraction at a certain finite time, and at that time the scale factor takes its maximum value $a_{\max}$. Find $a_{\max}$ and express it using $\varOmega_{\mathrm{m}}$.

Q5. Again let $t=0$ be the instant of the Big Bang as in Q4, and consider the case $\varOmega_{\mathrm{m}}=\varOmega_{\mathrm{m,\,max}}$. The present time $t_0$ is interpreted as the "age of the universe"; express $t_0$ using $H_0$. Further, using the value of $H_0$ given in Q3, find the value of $t_0$ to 2 significant figures. Take the unit of $t_0$ to be the year, and use

$$1\,\mathrm{year}=3.15\times10^{7}\,\mathrm{s}$$

The value of $t_0$ found in Q5 is much smaller than the value widely accepted at present as the age of the universe (about 13.8 billion years). In cosmology, a gas of particles with non-zero mass whose speeds are small compared with the speed of light is called "matter", and in [I] we considered a model of the universe containing only "matter" as energy density (a "matter-dominated universe"). From the result of Q5, this model is considered not to describe the real universe completely, which suggests the possibility that energy densities other than "matter" also exist in the real universe. In [II] and [III] let us consider this problem.

[II] Accelerating expansion of the universe and dark energy

In [I] we dealt only with the component of the energy density originating from "matter", but for a more general component of the energy density, which has a pressure and does work during expansion and contraction, the Friedmann equation is written, with $n$ a certain constant and $\varOmega'$ the density parameter of this component, as

$$\frac{H^2}{H_0^2}=\frac{\varOmega'}{a^n}+\frac{1-\varOmega'}{a^2} \qquad (\mathrm{II.1})$$

That is, the energy density $\varepsilon(t)$ considered here is given by

$$\varepsilon(t)=Ac^2\frac{\varOmega'}{a(t)^n}$$

($A$ is the positive constant given in Q3).

Again, as a simple mechanical model that can describe the expansion of the universe, consider the sphere of radius $R(t)=a(t)R_0$ considered in [I]. This time, however, assume that a uniform pressure acts. Regarding the expansion of the universe as an adiabatic process, the first law of thermodynamics can be expressed, with $p$ the pressure, $V$ the volume of the sphere, and $\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tot}}=\varepsilon V$ the energy inside the sphere ($\varepsilon$ is the energy density), as

$$\varDelta\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tot}}+p\varDelta V=0 \qquad (\mathrm{II.2})$$

Here $\varDelta\mathcal{E}_{\mathrm{tot}}$, $\varDelta V$ represent small changes of the energy inside the sphere and of the volume, respectively.

Q6. By dividing both sides of equation (II.2) by a small time interval $\varDelta t$ and then taking the limit $\varDelta t\to0$, express the rate of change with time of the energy density, $\dot{\varepsilon}$, using $p$, $\varepsilon$ and $H(t)$.

In cosmology, the equation for $\dot{\varepsilon}$ obtained here is called the "fluid equation".

A representative example of an energy density other than "matter" is electromagnetic waves, that is, a photon gas, which in cosmology is called "radiation". Here, assume that the number density of photons (number per unit volume) has the same dependence on $a$ as the energy density ($\propto$ mass density) of "matter" considered in Q3, and that the wavelength of the photons (electromagnetic waves) increases in proportion to the scale factor as the universe expands. This phenomenon is called the "redshift" due to cosmic expansion.

Q7. When the dependence of the energy density of "radiation", $\varepsilon_r$, on the scale factor $a$ is expressed as $\varepsilon_r\propto a^{-n}$, find $n$. Further, using the result of Q6, find the value of $w$ when the "equation of state" is written as $p=w\varepsilon$ ($w$ is a certain dimensionless constant).

Q8. Observational facts have shown that the present universe is undergoing accelerating expansion ($\ddot{a}>0$). By interpreting the Friedmann equation (II.1) as the law of conservation of mechanical energy (I.2), in the same way as in Q4, find the condition that the constant $n$ on the right-hand side of equation (II.1) must satisfy for accelerating expansion to be realized. Here assume $\varOmega'>0$. Also, for the equation of state $p=w\varepsilon$, find the condition on $w$ for the above condition on $n$ to be satisfied.

The discovery of the accelerating expansion of the universe is relatively recent, around the end of the 20th century. For this achievement, three people, Riess (A. G. Riess), Schmidt (B.P. Schmidt) and Perlmutter (S.Perlmutter), received the Nobel Prize in Physics in 2011. An energy density that causes such accelerating expansion is generally called "dark energy". In particular, a constant energy density with no dependence on $a$ (the case $n=0$ in equation (II.1)) is, for historical reasons, called the "cosmological constant", and is known as a representative example of dark energy. Dark energy other than the cosmological constant is sometimes called "quintessence" (the fifth force). As Q8 suggests, dark energy is a strange energy density that is accompanied by negative pressure, and therefore has the property that its energy increases as it expands adiabatically. From the discovery of accelerating expansion, it is thought that some kind of dark energy exists in our universe, but its true nature is still unknown.

[III] Dark energy and Einstein's static universe

Below, as an example of a case in which "matter" and dark energy (other than the cosmological constant) coexist, let us examine the following Friedmann equation:

$$\frac{H^2}{{H_0}^2}=\frac{\varOmega_{\mathrm{m}}}{a^3}+\frac{\varOmega_{\mathrm{d}}}{a}+\frac{1-\varOmega_{\mathrm{m}}-\varOmega_{\mathrm{d}}}{a^2} \qquad (\mathrm{III.1})$$

Here $\varOmega_{\mathrm{m}}$ and $\varOmega_{\mathrm{d}}$ are the density parameters of "matter" and of dark energy, respectively, and we assume $\varOmega_{\mathrm{m}}>0$, $\varOmega_{\mathrm{d}}>0$.

Q9. Interpreting the Friedmann equation (III.1) as the law of conservation of mechanical energy (I.2), in the same way as in Q4, find the function $U(a)$ and show the rough shape of its graph. Further, defining $a_{\mathrm{c}}$ as the value of the scale factor $a$ at which the expansion changes from decelerating expansion $\ddot{a}<0$ to accelerating expansion $\ddot{a}>0$, express the values of $a_{\mathrm{c}}$ and $U(a_{\mathrm{c}})$ using $\varOmega_{\mathrm{m}}$, $\varOmega_{\mathrm{d}}$, etc., and mark the position of $a_{\mathrm{c}}$ on the graph you drew. Here the origin of $U(a)$ is fixed so that $\displaystyle\lim_{a\to\infty}U(a)=0$ when $\varOmega_{\mathrm{d}}=0$.

Q10. As a dimensionless physical quantity representing the degree of accelerating expansion of the present universe, it is important to determine by observation the "acceleration parameter" $q$ defined by $q=\left.\dfrac{\ddot{a}a}{\dot{a}^2}\right|_{t=t_0}$, and this gives knowledge of the density parameters of the real universe. Suppose that $q=0.3$; assuming $\varOmega_{\mathrm{m}}+\varOmega_{\mathrm{d}}=1$ (a flat universe), find the values of $\varOmega_{\mathrm{m}}$ and $\varOmega_{\mathrm{d}}$.

Historically, the model of the universe first proposed by Einstein was a static universe in which the scale factor $a(t)$ does not depend on time ("Einstein's static universe"). Einstein introduced the cosmological constant in order to realize this model of the universe; here, based on the Friedmann equation (III.1), let us assume the existence of the above dark energy and look for a static-universe solution.

Q11. A static-universe solution is a solution of the Friedmann equation (III.1) satisfying $\dot{a}=\ddot{a}=0$ independently of $t$. Here, however, $a(t_0)=1$ and $H(t_0)\left(=\left.\dfrac{\dot{a}}{a}\right|_{t=t_0}\right)=H_0$ are not necessarily assumed to hold. With $\varOmega_{\mathrm{m}}=0.36$, find, to 2 significant figures, the value of $\varOmega_{\mathrm{d}}$ for which a static-universe solution exists, and the value $a_{\mathrm{s}}$ of the scale factor representing the static-universe solution.

Q12. Consider what happens when the universe deviates slightly from the static-universe solution $a(t)\equiv a_{\mathrm{s}}$ of the previous question, that is, when at a certain time $t_1$, $a(t_1)\fallingdotseq a_{\mathrm{s}}$, $a(t_1)\neq a_{\mathrm{s}}$, and explain it concisely. If necessary, you may use a simple figure or the like in your explanation.

Einstein considered the static-universe solution more than 10 years before the discovery of the expansion of the universe by Hubble and Lemaître, and, as stated above, Einstein's original motivation for introducing the cosmological constant (an example of dark energy) was to realize a static-universe solution. This model of the universe had a "shape" like a spherical surface and was very interesting, but with the discovery of the expansion of the universe it became clear that it does not fit the real universe. Thus the main motivation for which Einstein introduced the cosmological constant was lost, and for a long time the cosmological constant did not receive much attention. However, with the discovery of the accelerating expansion of the universe at the end of the 20th century, the existence of the cosmological constant, and more generally of dark energy, as the so-called "source of acceleration" of cosmic expansion, came into the spotlight.

problems.title: Problem 1: Synchronization phenomena — Kuramoto model
problems.problem:
Problem 1 (75 points)

Synchronization phenomena — Kuramoto model

Astonishing phenomena such as tens of thousands of fireflies flashing simultaneously, or the steps of a crowd walking on a suspension bridge spontaneously falling into step so that the bridge sways strongly, are due to "synchronization phenomena". Synchronization phenomena are also involved in life-sustaining activities such as the heartbeat and the body clock, and they hold the key to robot control systems; they are physical phenomena indispensable to our lives and to society. Their mechanism has been clarified by research in "nonlinear science".

Here we study a representative system of coupled phase oscillators step by step.

1 System of two oscillators

Consider a point moving in uniform circular motion with constant angular velocity $\omega$ on the circle of radius 1 centred at the origin of the $xy$ plane; its $x$ and $y$ coordinates are

$$\begin{aligned} x(t) &= \cos(\omega t+\alpha) \\ y(t) &= \sin(\omega t+\alpha) \end{aligned}$$

so it performs simple harmonic oscillation ($\alpha$ is the initial phase). Denoting the phase by $\theta(t)$,

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta}{\mathrm{d}t} = \omega$$

is satisfied. On the other hand, if the $xy$ plane is regarded as the complex plane, the point $(x, y)$ corresponds to the complex number $z = x + y\,i$. In this problem, "oscillator" means such a rotating oscillator.

Consider two oscillators $(x_1, y_1), (x_2, y_2)$ oscillating with angular velocities $\omega_1, \omega_2$. Denote the phases of the oscillators by $\theta_1(t), \theta_2(t)$:

$$\begin{aligned} x_1 &= \cos\theta_1, \quad y_1 = \sin\theta_1 \\ x_2 &= \cos\theta_2, \quad y_2 = \sin\theta_2 \end{aligned}$$

The uniform circular motions of the two oscillators are expressed by

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm{d}\theta_1}{\mathrm{d}t} &= \omega_1 \quad (\theta_1 = \omega_1 t + \alpha_1) \\ \frac{\mathrm{d}\theta_2}{\mathrm{d}t} &= \omega_2 \quad (\theta_2 = \omega_2 t + \alpha_2) \end{aligned}$$

Now suppose that each oscillator receives from the other oscillator an action of strength $K$ expressed by the following equations. Let $K > 0$.

$$\begin{aligned} \frac{\mathrm{d}\theta_1}{\mathrm{d}t} &= \omega_1 + \frac{K}{2}\sin(\theta_2-\theta_1) \\ \frac{\mathrm{d}\theta_2}{\mathrm{d}t} &= \omega_2 + \frac{K}{2}\sin(\theta_1-\theta_2) \end{aligned} \qquad (1)$$

The action that the oscillators exert on each other is called the interaction. With a view to treating a system of $N$ oscillators later, the factor $\frac{1}{2}$ is attached to the interaction term.

This interaction means that if one's own phase lags behind that of the partner, one's phase advances faster, and if one's own phase is ahead of that of the partner, one's phase advances more slowly.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-1-fig1.png

Q1 Writing the phase difference as $\phi = \theta_1 - \theta_2$, show that the derivative of the phase difference is given by the following relation:

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}}{\mathrm{d}t}\phi = \mathit{\Delta}\omega - K\sin\phi$$

where $\mathit{\Delta}\omega = \omega_1 - \omega_2$.

Q2 Derive the condition that $K, \mathit{\Delta}\omega$ must satisfy for a solution to exist in which the phase difference is constant in time.

Q3 Find the value $\phi^*$ of $\phi$ when the phase difference has become constant (fixed point), in terms of $K, \mathit{\Delta}\omega$. In general there are two fixed points; discuss the stability of each.

[Hint] It suffices to examine the direction of change when $\phi$ deviates by a small amount from the fixed point. Use the fact that, for a function $f(x)$, when $|h|$ is sufficiently small,

$$f(a+h) \fallingdotseq f(a) + f'(a)h$$

is a valid approximation.

2 System of $N$ oscillators and the order parameter

We extend to a system of $N$ oscillators, each having angular frequency $\omega_1, \cdots, \omega_N$. Assuming that each oscillator receives interactions from the other oscillators, its equation, extending equation (1), is given by

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta_j}{\mathrm{d}t} = \omega_j + \frac{K}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N}\sin(\theta_k-\theta_j), \quad j = 1, \cdots N, \qquad (2)$$

To visualize the dynamical behaviour of the phases, it is convenient to imagine a group of points running around the unit circle in the complex plane and to consider the quantity defined as follows:

$$re^{i\psi} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{k=1}^{N} e^{i\theta_k} \qquad (3)$$

This quantity is called the (complex) order parameter. $r$ and $\psi$ are real numbers with $r \geqq 0$. The magnitude (absolute value) of the complex number computed on the right-hand side is $r$, and its phase (argument) is $\psi$. Here the relation obtained by extending the exponential function to complex numbers (Euler's formula)

$$e^{i\theta} = \cos\theta + i\sin\theta$$

is used. $\theta$ is a real number, and this formula relates the exponential function to the trigonometric functions.

Q4 Show that $r = 1$ when all phases $\theta_k$ are equal.

Q5 Consider the case where the phases of the oscillators are equally spaced and $N$ is sufficiently large. The phases can then be regarded as distributed continuously and uniformly from $0$ to $2\pi$; show, using an integral, that $r = 0$. Note that the integral of a complex-valued function can be defined in the same way as the integral of a real-valued function. Splitting the complex values into real and imaginary parts, computing each integral as an integral of a real function and adding the results gives the integral of the complex-valued function.

Q6 There are 10 oscillators, and at a certain instant their positions are given by the black dots in the following figure (complex plane). Mark the approximate position of the order parameter $re^{i\psi}$ of equation (3) in the figure on the answer sheet. State the reason for choosing that position.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-1-fig2.png

Q7 Show that, using the quantities defined in equation (3), equation (2) can be written as

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta_j}{\mathrm{d}t} = \omega_j + Kr\sin(\psi-\theta_j), \quad j = 1, \cdots N \qquad (4)$$

Equation (4) shows that the time evolution of each oscillator $\theta_j$ is determined by its action with the whole oscillator system through the order parameter. The interaction with the other oscillators $\theta_k$ is replaced by an interaction with an average field.

3 Self-consistent equation and critical point

Now let us consider steady solutions. That is, consider the case where the solutions $\theta_j(t)$ $(j = 1, \cdots, N)$ of equation (2) move steadily as a whole, and the order parameter defined by equation (3) rotates on a circle of constant radius $r$ with constant angular velocity $\mathit{\Omega}$ (then $\psi = \mathit{\Omega}t$). Using the variables $\theta_j^* = \theta_j - \mathit{\Omega}t$, $\omega_j^* = \omega_j - \mathit{\Omega}$ (this amounts to considering a coordinate system rotating with angular frequency $\mathit{\Omega}$), equation (4) becomes

$$\frac{\mathrm{d}\theta_j^*}{\mathrm{d}t} = \omega_j^* - Kr\sin\theta_j^*, \quad j = 1, \cdots N \qquad (5)$$

and from now on we examine equation (5).

Consider the case where the number of oscillators $N$ is very large, and suppose that a sum over the oscillators $\dfrac{1}{N}\displaystyle\sum_{k=1}^{N}\cdots$ is expressed, using the distribution function of $\omega_k^*$, as $\displaystyle\int g(\omega^*)\cdots\mathrm{d}\omega^*$. Further, suppose that $\omega_k$ is distributed around the angular frequency $\mathit{\Omega}$ of the mean motion, and that the distribution function $g(\omega^*)$ of the deviation from $\mathit{\Omega}$ is a function symmetric about $\omega^* = 0$ with its peak at $\omega^* = 0$, having a form such as, for example, the Gaussian distribution (normal distribution)

$$g(x) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{2\pi}\sigma}\exp\Big(-\frac{x^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big)$$

or the Lorentz distribution

$$g(x) = \frac{1}{\pi}\frac{\gamma}{x^2+\gamma^2}$$

By an argument similar to Q2 and Q3, it is known that the oscillators contributing to the stable steady solution are those with $|\omega_k^*| \leqq Kr$, so the order parameter $r$ is computed in the rotating coordinate system as

$$r = \int_{-Kr}^{Kr} e^{i\theta^*(\omega^*)} g(\omega^*)\,\mathrm{d}\omega^* \qquad (6)$$

where $\omega^* = Kr\sin\theta^*$.

Q8 Show that equation (6) can be written as

$$r = Kr\int_{-\pi/2}^{\pi/2} g(Kr\sin\theta^*)\cos^2\theta^*\,\mathrm{d}\theta^* \qquad (7)$$

Equation (7) has the form of an equation for finding a state in which the sought solution $(r)$ finally agrees, without contradiction, with itself through the other physical quantities derived from that solution, and it is called a self-consistent equation.

Now let us consider the condition for synchronization to occur. Equation (7) always has the solution $r = 0$. The existence of another solution is the condition for synchronization to occur.

Q9 When $K$ is larger than a certain value $K_{\mathrm{c}}$, a solution other than $r = 0$ exists. By expanding equation (7) assuming that $(Kr\sin\theta^*)$ is small, express this $K_{\mathrm{c}}$ in terms of $g(0)$. Since we are considering for $g(\omega^*)$ a function with its peak at $\omega^* = 0$, $g''(0) < 0$.

[Hint] The approximation for the function $f(x)$ shown in Q3 is the first-order approximation in $h$ for sufficiently small $|h|$; here it is useful to go one step further and use the second-order approximation

$$f(a+h) \fallingdotseq f(a) + f'(a)h + \frac{f''(a)}{2}h^2$$

4 Analogy with the phase transition of a magnetic material

In discussing the phase transition of a magnetic material, arguments similar to those used so far for the coupled phase oscillator model are used. If a magnetic material is regarded as a collection of microscopic particles with magnetic properties, it is difficult to treat the many-particle problem exactly, so the interaction received from the other individual microscopic magnets is approximated by an average interaction. Calculating by the methods of statistical thermodynamics, the magnetization $m$ of the magnetic material is expressed, as a function of the assumed $m$, as

$$m = \tanh\Big(\frac{zJm}{k_{\mathrm{B}}T}\Big) \qquad (8)$$

This equation is a self-consistent equation for $m$. Here $J$ is the strength of the interaction, $T$ the absolute temperature, $k_{\mathrm{B}}$ the Boltzmann constant, and $z$ a constant depending on the structure of the magnetic material. $\tanh(x)$ is the function defined by

$$\tanh(x) = \frac{e^x-e^{-x}}{e^x+e^{-x}}$$

and for $|x| \ll 1$ it is expanded as

$$\tanh x = x - \frac{1}{3}x^3 + \cdots$$

Q10 Equation (8) always has the solution $m = 0$, but with a certain temperature $T_{\mathrm{c}}$ as the boundary, the number of possible solutions changes from one to three. Express $k_{\mathrm{B}}T_{\mathrm{c}}$ in terms of $J, z$. It is useful to consider the expansion of the function $\tanh x$ up to the $x^3$ term. If necessary, explain using a graph.

Q11 Writing the solution $m$ when it has a solution other than $0$ in the previous question as $m_0$, show that in the temperature range where the temperature $T$ is lower than $T_c$ and sufficiently close to $T_c$, $|m_0|$ rises in proportion to $(T_{\mathrm{c}}-T)^{\beta}$, that is,

$$|m_0| = C\,(T_{\mathrm{c}}-T)^{\beta}$$

and find $\beta$. $C$ is a certain constant.

In Q9 we found the critical point by solving the self-consistent equation of the coupled phase oscillator model. On the other hand, in Q10 we found the phase transition point (critical point) of the magnetic material by solving a self-consistent equation of very similar structure in the problem of the phase transition of a magnetic material. The behaviour near the critical point in Q11 can be discussed in the same way for the coupled phase oscillator model.

The coupled phase oscillator model considered here (Coupled Phase Oscillator Model) has become a powerful tool for understanding synchronization phenomena and collective behaviour in a wide range of fields such as physics, engineering, biology and sociology, and it is called the Kuramoto model after its proposer, Yoshiki Kuramoto, Professor Emeritus of Kyoto University.

The Boltzmann Medal, an international prize in statistical physics, is awarded at the International Conference on Statistical Physics held once every three years; Kuramoto received the 2025 Boltzmann Medal for pioneering a methodology that enables universal and simple descriptions of the diverse and complex phenomena seen in non-equilibrium systems.

problems.title: Problem 2: Induction motor
problems.problem:
Problem 2 (75 points)

Induction motor

A machine that converts electric power into work is called a motor (electric motor). Here we examine the principle and characteristics of the widely used induction motor.

1 Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction

In Faraday's law of electromagnetic induction (1), when the magnetic flux $\Phi(t)$ through a coil at time $t$ changes in time, an induced electromotive force $V(t)$ arises in the coil, proportional to the time derivative of $\Phi(t)$:

$$V(t) = -\frac{\mathrm{d}\Phi(t)}{\mathrm{d}t} \qquad (1)$$

Here the minus sign on the right-hand side indicates that the direction of the electromotive force produced is the direction that induces a current in the direction opposing the change in flux. This Faraday's law holds as it is even when the coil itself deforms or moves. Let us verify this with a simple example.

As in Fig. 1, in a space where there is a uniform magnetic field pointing vertically downward with magnetic flux density $B$, two conducting rails are laid parallel on a horizontal plane at a distance $d$ apart, and a conducting rod is placed on them. The two rails are connected at the left end and, together with the conducting rod, form a single closed circuit. These conductors have electrical resistance. The conducting rod is moved to the right with velocity $v$. We now find the electromotive force produced in the circuit in two ways. Let the magnitude of the elementary charge be $e$, and ignore the effect of the magnetic field produced by the current flowing in the circuit.

https://raw.githubusercontent.com/Eisatopon/physics-olympiads-bank/main/images/jpho-2026-2-fig1.png

Fig. 1.

Q1 The electrons in the moving conducting rod receive a Lorentz force from the magnetic field; if this force is interpreted as a force due to an electric field produced in the circuit, an electromotive force can be regarded as having arisen in the circuit. What are the magnitude of this Lorentz force and the magnitude of the electromotive force? Is the direction of the induced current arrow a or b in Fig. 1?
